2365.tone: Three-level tone language: 'There are three tone levels, H[igh], M[id], and L[ow]. Contour tones on single syllables are HL, HM, LH, and MH' (p. 48); 'There are no ML- or LM-toned syllables.' Lexical tone melodies on noun stems (/L/, /HL/, /LHL/, /M/, /HM/, /LHM(L)/...), suffixal tone partly lexical, M-Spreading, tone sandhi (sec. 3.8.3), grammatical tone on postpositions. El cambio de acento hacia la primera sílaba se presenta en aquellas palabras cuya composición silábica es más compleja, palabras de tres o cuatro sílabas, el acento de intensidad ocurre en la primera sílaba.

2368.prule: None. Lexical tone language (Djenné: two tone levels H/L; Cliffs: three levels H/M/L) with stem-level tone melodies. The grammarian states that there is no well-defined stress system, that tones do not behave as pitch-accent markers, that a pitch-accent analysis is unattractive/unsupported (stems may have zero or two tonal peaks), and that there is no weight-sensitive word-level accentual system.
2368.quote: Djenne grammar sec. 3.1.2, pp.19-20: "Since syncope and accentual processes are rare in J-S of Djenné, there is not much to say about foot structure. Stem-level tone melodies have a weak resemblance to pitch-accent, since there is rarely more than one H-toned peak on a stem. /LHL/ is a common lexical melody, but /HLH/ is rare in uncompounded stems ... 2368.tone: Djenné: two lexical tone levels (H, L); stem-level melodies with rarely more than one H peak (/LHL/ common, /HLH/ rare), but stems of any size can be all-L or all-H and Tone Leveling makes whole compounds all-H or all-L, so the author rejects a pitch-accent analysis. Cliffs: three tone levels (H, M, L); /L/ stems have no tonal peak, /H/ stems are stem-wide H with no accented syllable, /MLH/ stems have two peaks; pitch-accent rejected. Weight enters only tonal processes (imperfective tone drop in Djenné; floating-H spreading blocked at first syllable of heavy CvCvCv stems in Cliffs). Word-/phrase-final intonation effects (falling HL at prosodic breaks) are described separately in sec. 3.7.

tn.quote: J-S of Djenné has two phonemic tone levels, versus three in Cliffs. The two tonemes are H[igh] and L[ow]. An individual syllable may be H, L, <HL>, <LH>, or <LHL>. All of these are possible with Cvv syllables (46). … Although there are only two tone levels at the lexical level, at the phonetic level one can speak of mid pitch as opposed to high and low. … In addition, H-toned stems and particles are phonetically downstepped in two positions: a) after an LH-toned word (§3.6.5.1), and b) at the end of intonation phrases following another H-toned word (§3.6.5.2).

2369.dq: 加茂话常用的词头 kɯ³¹、mɯ³¹都可构成类属广泛的附加式合成词，此时两者要变读为轻声①。 [fn.①] 文中轻声标 0 调。 … 加茂话的一些词在语流当中，……这些词在语流中一般都降低音高，变读为 33 调。 (The prefix neutral-tone statement is word-internal; the function-word lowering is in connected speech 语流. Neither is a stress statement, so no stress domain is stated.)
2369.dloc: p.83 para.2 (five-tone inventory); p.84 sec.一(一) last two paragraphs + fn.① (prefixes kɯ-/mɯ- read as 轻声 neutral tone, written tone 0); p.84 sec.二 para.1 (function words 55->33 in connected speech); p.86 sec.二(四) (sandhi tone 'lighter' than citation tone)
2369.prule: Tone language: five lexical tones (55, 51, 31, 33, 11) on full syllables; morphological/semantic/syntactic tone sandhi never creates new tone values; no word-stress rule is stated anywhere in the source. The only word-prosodic statement: the grammaticalized prefixes kɯ- (< numeral 'one', citation tone 31) and mɯ- (citation 31) are read in neutral tone (轻声, written tone 0) before the full-toned root in affixal compounds (kɯ⁰det⁵⁵ 'jump', mɯ⁰thum⁵⁵ 'pomegranate'), i.e. prefix+root words are atonic+toned (weak-strong, root-final prominence).
2369.quote: [p.83] 加茂话有 5 个声调：高平调 55、高降调 51、中降调 31、中平调 33 和低平调 11，变调不产生新调值。总体来说，加茂话的变调模式有词法变调、句义变调和句法变调三种。 … [p.84] 但它们仍未完全虚化成表形态的词头，所以依靠音高的变化体现这一语义功能。若语义进一步虚化，则其可能伴随着语音的轻声化，进而语法化为类别标记。加茂话常用的词头 kɯ³¹、mɯ³¹都可构成类属广泛的附加式合成词，此时两者要变读为轻声①。kɯ³¹来源于数字“一”，是加茂话中最能产的词头，指称范畴较为宽泛，可构成不同语义类别的词类，例如：kɯ⁰det⁵⁵“蹦”、kɯ⁰laːu⁵⁵“圆”、kɯ⁰tek⁵⁵“壁虎”、kɯ⁰ziau¹¹“明天”、kɯ⁰tsa⁵¹“菠萝”、kɯ⁰siak⁵⁵“垃圾”等。mɯ³¹本义不明，主要构成果菜类及粮食类名词，例如：mɯ⁰thum⁵⁵“石榴”、mɯ⁰luəŋ⁵⁵“槟榔”、mɯ⁰ŋou⁵⁵“糯稻”等。随着语义的彻底虚化，这两个词头已经变成了一种语法标记。 [fn.①] 文中轻声标 0 调。 … [p.84 sec.二] 加茂话的一些词在语流当中，不管前后相邻音节的语音条件如何，都以自身本调为条件发生变调，一律由高平调 55 调变成中平调 33 调，变调规则较为固定。人称代词 kau⁵⁵“我”、məi⁵⁵“你”、au⁵⁵“我们”、tei⁵⁵“咱们”、sau⁵⁵…

2369.idn: 黎语加茂方言, called 加茂话 'Jiamao speech' in the article: one of the five Li (Hlai) dialects (侾, 杞, 本地, 美孚, 加茂), said to differ greatly from the other four and to be mutually unintelligible with them; data: Fieldsite: 海南省保亭黎族苗族自治县加茂镇加答村委会金不弄村…
2369.exq_: 但它们仍未完全虚化成表形态的词头，所以依靠音高的变化体现这一语义功能。 (Class-name first members of 类名+专名 compounds, e.g. naːm⁵⁵⁻³³hɔːt⁵¹ 'snot', lower 55->33 but are explicitly said not yet to be 轻声; only kɯ-/mɯ- are atonic. No stress rule, so no stress exceptions.)
2369.tone: Source is a tone-sandhi study. 5 tones 55/51/31/33/11 (p.83); Norquest 2007:335 gives the register values A 55/11, X 51/31, DL 53/31, DS 55/22 after Ouyang & Zheng 1983. The words 重音/重读/轻重音 (stress) never occur in Wu 2020 (whole text read); Norquest 2007 ch.5 and Thurgood 1992 also carry no synchronic stress/accent statement for Jiamao. What the source does say about prominence: (a) prefixes kɯ-/mɯ- are 轻声 'neutral tone', written tone 0 (p.84 + fn.①); (b) 55-tone function words (pronouns, adverb na, conjunction bɛ, preposition haŋ, localizers, copula tsaŋ, 'go' hai, negator ŋɔ) drop to 33 in connected speech unless emphatic, and citation tone marks emphasis (pp.84-86); (c) 'the sandhi tone is lighter (变轻), the tone of voice milder' (p.86). None of this is a lexical stress rule.

2370.dq: 太谷の二音節語の第二音節には軽声はなく,軽声はいくつかの語末・文末にのみ現われる。 [The second syllable of Taigu disyllabic words has no neutral tone; neutral tone appears only in a few word-final and sentence-final items.] (p.25) — statements are about disyllabic lexical words (二音節語, 二字組) in elicitation; fn.6 adds that the stress-type minimal pairs differ only in sentence-final position (文末の環境に限り).
2370.dloc: p.25: end of §4 (right column) and opening of §5 二字組連読変調 (below Table 3); footnotes 5-6 on pp.30-31.
2370.prule: No word-stress rule. Taigu is a five-tone lexical-tone system (Table 3 headers on p.25: 平声 33, 上声 412, 去声 452, 陰入 ʔ3, 陽入 ʔ412) with two-syllable tone sandhi; the only prominence facts stated are about neutral tone (軽声, destressed toneless syllables): the second syllable of ordinary disyllabic words is NOT neutral-toned; neutral tone appears only on a few word-/sentence-final items (桌子, 我的, 甚嚒), realised like the short yin-ru tone; some sandhi combinations have a 'B pattern' in which the second syllable is 'pronounced lightly'; Putonghua full-tone vs neutral-tone minimal pairs (編排 biānpái/biānpai etc.) are distinguished only sentence-finally, the weak member having both syllables lower and the second syllable shorter and slightly falling. Where weakening occurs it is on the final syllable (initial prominence), but it is marginal and lexically restricted, not a positional stress rule.
2370.quote: 軽声について楊氏は,{太谷城関話にも軽声はあるが,その範囲は「普通話」ほど大きくない。太谷の二音節語の第二音節には軽声はなく,軽声はいくつかの語末・文末にのみ現われる。例えば,桌子・我的・甚嚒などなどで,聴いたところ陰入調に極めて近い。}と述べているが,5) 黄氏の発音では,これらは皆陰入と全く同一である。6) ... 組み合わせによっては変調のパターンを2通り有する場合が存在するが,その場合には,第二音節が軽く発音されると考えられる方をBパターンと呼び,そうでない方をAパターンと呼ぶことにする。 [fn.6, pp.30-31] ただ,黄氏の発音において,次の如き平声+平声のミニマルペアは,文末の環境に限り,上段の意味の場合には2音節とも比較的高く且つ長く発音され,下段の意味の場合には2音節とも比較的低く,特に第2音節は短くやや下降気味に発音されるようである。(カッコ内は「普通話」の相当する拼音。) 編排 [pieN33 p'ai33] 〈動〉排列する,編成する (biānpái) 〈動〉根も葉もないことで人を中傷する (biānpai) 東西 ... 〈名〉東西 (dōngxī) 〈名〉物 (dōngxi)

2370.exq_: No stress rule is stated. The exceptions to the 'no neutral-tone second syllable' statement are listed: 軽声はいくつかの語末・文末にのみ現われる。例えば,桌子・我的・甚嚒などなど (p.25); plus the lexically restricted B sandhi pattern (第二音節が軽く発音されると考えられる方をBパターンと呼び, p.25) and the sentence-final-only minimal pairs of fn.6.
2370.tone: Lexical tone language: five citation tones in Taigu (Higuchi Table 3, p.25: 平声 33, 上声 412, 去声 452, 陰入 ʔ3, 陽入 ʔ412; Yang 1983 gives 去声 as 45), with an A/B two-pattern disyllabic sandhi system. On stress the source says only: (i) Taigu has neutral tone but far less than Putonghua; the second syllable of disyllabic words is not neutral-toned; neutral tone is limited to a few word-/sentence-final items realised like yin-ru (Yang 1983 quoted, p.25) and in Higuchi's speaker identical to yin-ru; (ii) the B sandhi pattern is the one where the second syllable is 'pronounced lightly' (p.25); (iii) fn.6: Beijing-type full-tone vs neutral-tone minimal pairs (編排, 東西, 飢荒, 精神) are distinguished only sentence-finally, the weak member having both syllables lower and the second syllable shorter and slightly falling. Yagi 2019 pp.120-122: neutral-tone rate on 81 items is 1% in Qixian and Xiaoyi, 21% in Taigu, 52% at the northern (Shanyin) and southern (Yuncheng) ends of Shanxi; Taiyuan shows no systematic word-final sandhi in non-reduplicated words (太原などの一部方言では非畳語において体系的な語末変調がみられず, p.122); fn.6 (p.132) refers to Iwata 1999/2001 on leftward stress shift (ストレスの左移動) in northern dialects, not to a Jin-specific rule.

tn.translation: 4. Citation tones. The tone categories and tone values of the citation tones are as in Table 1. [Table 1: ping 33, shang 412, qu 452, yin-ru 3 (-ʔ coda), yang-ru 412 (-ʔ coda)] Ping and yin-ru are identical in pitch, but yin-ru is shorter than ping and the [-ʔ] is quite clearly audible. 2371.prule: Word-tone language: four contrastive word-level tone patterns (high vs low pitch, with tense vs breathy voice register, on the initial syllable x non-falling vs falling contour over the whole phonological word). Stress is a tone-dependent correlate, not an independent positional system: 'word-initial stress is the norm'; in words of three or more syllables and in suffixed words carrying the falling-contour patterns (3, 4), the contour is modified to rising and primary stress shifts 'in general' from the initial to the word-final syllable; words with non-falling contour (patterns 1, 2) keep initial primary stress. Position therefore depends on the word's lexical tone pattern and its morphology, not on syllable count or weight.

2371.tone: Four contrastive tone patterns numbered 1-4, written as superscript digits (Table 39, p. 861, monosyllables: la¹ 'wages' = high pitch, non-falling contour / la³ 'steam' = high, falling / la² 'mountain' = low, non-falling / la⁴ 'work' = low, falling; Table 40, p. 862, disyllables: chomu¹ 'sister-in-law' / chomu³ 'a specific day' / phumu² 'daughter' / chyomu⁴ 'hen'): patterns 1 and 3 high pitch with tense (modal) voice, 2 and 4 low pitch with lax/breathy voice; pitch level 'confined to the initial syllable of the word, while the contour spreads over the whole word'; non-falling (level/rising) vs falling contour; word-initial voiced stops and affricates occur only with low tone. In trisyllabic and affixed words the falling contour of patterns 3 and 4 is replaced by a rising one (sec. 6.3), and the stress shift to the final syllable accompanies this: 'Without the change of stress to the word-final syllable, tone patterns 3 and 4, with the falling contour modified to rising, would be even more difficult to distinguish from the tone patterns 1 and 2 with a rising contour' (p. 863). Stress is thus described as initial by default and shifted to final as a function of the word's tone pattern; no weight or syllable-count conditioning.

2376.heavy: Only within [+ATR] HH disyllables: 'In HH words, the primary stress is carried by the first syllable if the second syllable is open, but if the second syllable of HH words is closed, it bears the primary stress.' Closed second syllables in [-ATR] words ('gʊ.lʊŋ, 'kʊ.kʊm) and in HF words ('ki.git, 'ke.kan) do not attract stress, so weight is not a general conditioning factor.
2376.dflt: initial (HH words with an open second syllable, all HF words, all [-ATR] words)
2376.prule: Word stress is a lexical property of each word ('In sum, words have their own stress pattern in Julut'): primary stress (correlate = intensity: loudness, pitch, vowel length) sits on the syllable carrying the 'presumed' high pitch, and that pitch pattern (HH / LH / HF among [+ATR] words) is declared non-phonemic and is not stated to be derivable from segmental shape (C's inference from Tables 2.15-2.16: ka.'bal HH vs 'ki.git HF, both CV.CVC). Disyllabic nouns only: [-ATR] (LL/LF) nouns always initial ('kɑ.rɑl, 'gʊ.lʊŋ, 'gʊ.lɪk, 'kʊ.kʊm...); [+ATR] LH nouns final (kar.'d̪o 'garden', ge.'let 'teeth'), HF nouns initial ('ga.la 'belly', 'ki.git 'thorn', 'ke.kan 'forehead', 'gi.t̪i 'termite hill'), HH nouns initial unless the second syllable is closed, then final ('wa.li 'wife', 'ga.t̪a, 'ko.bo, 'kpa.ya vs ka.'bal 'animal', ka.'ral, gu.'lun, gu.'lak). Same-shape pairs with different stress: ka.'bal (HH) vs 'ki.git (HF), both CV.CVC; ka.'ral [+ATR] 'passing' vs 'kɑ.rɑl [-ATR] 'durra part'.

2377.prule: Two-register tone language (H vs L, unmarked). Unbounded system with default to the right edge (sec. 1.3.2, Hayes 1995 terms); formalised in sec. 1.3.6 as quantity-sensitive unbounded feet + tonal prominence (H > L) + End Rule Left.

tn.quote: O juruna é definido como uma língua tonal. … No juruna, cada sílaba apresenta apenas um tom significativo (há línguas com mais de um tom por sílaba), e esse tom pode ser pontual ou glide … Dessa forma, resta a hipótese, mais provável, de uma língua de sistema de registro, com glides como variantes. tn.translation: Juruna is defined as a tonal language. … In Juruna each syllable carries only one significant tone (there are languages with more than one tone per syllable), and this tone may be level or a glide … Thus the most probable hypothesis remains: a register-system language, with glides as variants. Tones occurring phonetically in Juruna: high, mid, low (unmarked), falling and rising. Phonologically, as will be explained later, there are only high tone and low tone (unmarked).

2379.prule: The descriptions disagree on placement. Mathew 1887 (Kabi proper, first-hand): disyllabic substantives accented 'almost invariably on the first syllable'; nothing on longer words. Watson 1944 (first-hand Kabi from the Mary River; rule stated for his Kabi, Yugarabul, Wakka and Yugumbir vocabularies, the Kabi entries accent-marked, e.g. Ba'niraman, Bam'gina, Bi'dhal'ithin): 'Accent is generally on the first syllable and, to a lesser degree, on the third', with 'some exceptions' (a first syllable in -r is obscured and run into the second: kurū'man 'kangaroo'). Holmer 1983 (group-level for all seven Wakka-group languages incl. Kabi-Kabi and Batjala; no competent Kabi-Kabi speaker, no Kabi form cited): stress 'not significant' (non-distinctive); 'a certain tendency... everywhere' to stress the second syllable in words or utterances of some length, stress units possibly spanning two words (place names Cutháraba, Didíllibah); Goedemans 1998 App. D files Gabi-Gabi under 'stress is on the second syllable' on Holmer's authority alone. Initial (Mathew, Watson) vs peninitial (Holmer/StressTyp) for words of three or more syllables; the rule string codes Watson's first-hand Kabi statement (primary on the first syllable, lesser accent on the third).

2382.dq: In words where no syllabic accent is used the stress of the voice always rests on the first syllable of a word ... 3.—In words of more than two syllables the accent, as a general rule, rests on the last syllable but one (penultimate).
2382.dloc: Part I, 'General Rules relating to Accent, &c.', rules 2-3, p. 7.
2382.heavy: Source gives a hedged, partial denial of weight-sensitivity rather than an explicit one: 'This rule holds good even in words where the second (or later) syllable of a word contains a long vowel whilst the first syllable has only a short one, accent being to some extent independent of the quantity of vowel sounds; e.g., "Mosá" (tiger) = "mo′sá," &c.' (p. 7). 'To some extent' leaves room for vowel quantity to matter elsewhere; no weight-conditioned rule is stated anywhere in the accent section, and Endle's orthography does mark vowel length (á, ú) so quantity was a category he recognised.
2382.prule: Penultimate, quantity-insensitive, stated with a hedge: rule 3 'In words of more than two syllables the accent, as a general rule, rests on the last syllable but one (penultimate)' (p. 7); rule 2 gives initial accent for words with no written accent mark ('always rests on the first syllable'), which for disyllables coincides with penult (fai′dang, mo′sá, khàt′-bai, Tháng′nŭ), and is 'to some extent independent of the quantity of vowel sounds' (mo′sá: short first vowel accented over a long second). Rules 2+3 together give a uniform penultimate grid; most of Endle's accented citation forms fit it (fai′dang, mo′sá, Mosá′ni, khàt-láng′-bai, ga-glai′-nŭ, ge-le′-nŭ, ga-glai′-nai, ga-glai-nai′-sŭi, Guru′ï, main accent of Tháng′-ni-áu″-nŭ). Stated counterexamples: fai′dangman (3 syllables, initial; Endle's own rule-2 example, a conjugated verb), găzá′/Găfút′/Gădat′ (gă- adjectives, final), Gădet′siná (4 syllables, accent on the 2nd).
2382.srule: Secondary accent exists but no placement rule is given: 'In longer words we sometimes have two accented syllables'; Endle writes the main accent ″ and the secondary ′, word by word; his one example Tháng′-ni-áu″-nŭ 'even while going' has the main accent on the 3rd syllable (penult before enclitic nŭ) and the secondary on the 1st (root) syllable.

2382.tone: Endle 1884 never mentions tone anywhere in the accent section or the pronunciation chapter. The modern continuation of Endle's Darrang Plains Kachari is Boro/Bodo (Glottolog bodo1269, not a separate entry here and not in the catalog), analysed as a two-tone language: Joseph & Burling 2006 (Kokrajhar Boro, high/low tone contrast, one tone per word; no stress statement) and Das & Mahanta 2019: 3 (in the copy consulted): 'As far as Boro is concerned, apart from Hyman's arguments, the attributes of stress are also not entirely clear and therefore Boro is not amenable to an analysis as a pitch-accent language where lexical tone is delimited to the vicinity of the stressed syllable.' Endle's 'accent'/'cadence' marks may therefore partly encode pitch; this record codes what the 1884 source states, and the tone facts are for the rule-grade audit.

2383.prule: No word-stress placement rule is stated. Jinghpaw is a syllable-tone language (4 tones on open/sonorant-final syllables: high-level, mid-level, low-falling, high-falling; 2 on stop-final syllables). Native words are mono- or disyllabic; about 74% of disyllables are sesquisyllabic (Cə- minor syllable + full syllable), and the minor syllable 'has no tone' and 'has no stress'; syllabic-nasal presyllables are likewise toneless and 'often pronounced unstressed'. Prominence therefore falls on the final full, tone-bearing syllable of such words (an iambic / right-dominant pattern in Kurabe's later English papers), but the source gives no rule for the minority of full-syllable disyllables (ɡùmrà type) or for compounds.
2383.srule: Not mentioned in Kurabe 2012, sec. 3 音韻 pp.66-75 (the only stress statements are negative: Cə minor syllables 'have no stress', syllabic-nasal presyllables 'often pronounced unstressed'); nor in Kurabe 2017, 2018, 2020, 2021.

2383.tone: Syllable-tone language: 4 tones on smooth syllables (/má/ [55], /ma/ [33], /mà/ [31], /mâ/ [51]: yó 'plan', yo 'float', yò 'weaken', yô sentence-final particle), 2 on checked syllables (ɡát 'market' vs ɡàt 'run'); the high-falling tone is rare and largely secondary (kin terms, interjections, final particles, or derived from low-falling by prefixation). Minor syllables (Cə-) and syllabic nasals carry no tone and no stress. Kurabe 2017 (Onsei Kenkyu) analyses the light presyllable as an 'unstressed (light) position' with a reduced tone inventory and calls the disyllabic word shape 'iambic (right-dominant)'; Kurabe 2021 (AALL 15:48): 'Jinghpaw is a syllable-tone language with an iambic prosodic pattern.' The ILCAA textbook (2020:15) says the language 'prefers a ta-TAN rather than TAN-ta rhythm'. No source held states a stress algorithm over full syllables; the colonial grammars (Hanson 1896 initial vs Hertz 1902 final for full disyllables) disagree and do not separate tone from stress.

tn.translation: It has syllable tone, and in open syllables has four tones: high-level, mid-level, low-falling and high-falling. However, in closed syllables with a stop final consonant only two tones, High and Low, contrast. In this paper the four Jinghpaw tones are written /má/ [55], /ma/ [33], /mà/ [31], /mâ/ [51]: yó 'plan', yo 'float', yò 'weaken', yô (sentence-final particle 'yo, ne') (cf. ɡát 'market', ɡàt 'run'). Among the four tones the proportion of the high-falling tone is extremely low. ... Nevertheless, since minimal pairs exist as noted above, the high-falling tone must also be recognised as an independent toneme.

ev.text: Embora os Griffiths, 1976: 144, mencionem que o acento é previsível em Kadiwéu, não encontramos confirmação desta afirmativa nos dados por nós recolhidos. Por isso, consideramos o acento de intensidade imprevisível, ora incindindo sobre a primeira sílaba da raiz dos substantivos e verbos, ora sobre a segunda, não havendo nenhuma evidência de condicionamento fonológico. A TONICIDADE tem significância ou valor morfofonêmico e está por isto mesmo fora do foco de interesse deste trabalho. 2388.dq: dass der Ton nur auf einer der drei letzten Wortsilben ... ruht ... den Accent nur in wenigen speziellen Fällen auf der letzten, sonst stets auf der vorletzten oder drittletzten Silbe des Wortes.
2388.dloc: Separatum pp. 37-39 (= Sitzungsberichte [87]-[89]) of archive.org item diekafasprachein00rein; separatum pages 37-39 read.
2388.heavy: 'deren Vocal die übrigen an Gehalt überwigt': the vowel of a closed syllable outweighs that of an open one ('Der Vocal einer geschlossenen Silbe überwigt hinsichtlich der Betonung den einer offenen'); a long vowel outweighs a short one ('wenn deren Vocal an Gewicht den der drittletzten übertrifft', 'der auslautende Vocal lang'); a doubly closed syllable outweighs a singly closed one ('worin á, ó in der doppelt geschlossenen Silbe die Vocale in der penultima, nur einfach geschlossen, überwigen').
2388.dflt: Disyllables: penult regardless of weight. Longer words with penult and antepenult of equal weight: penult if the final vowel is long, antepenult if the final vowel is short.
2388.prule: Accent falls on one of the last three syllables of the word, on the syllable whose vowel outweighs the others in 'Gehalt/Gewicht' (weight): a closed syllable outweighs an open one, a long vowel a short one, a doubly closed syllable a singly closed one. Disyllabic vowel-final words: penult, regardless of vowel length (níhō, índē, búšō, búšē). Three or more syllables: penult if its vowel outweighs the antepenult's (baqérō, aríngō, boqúallō), or if penult and antepenult are of equal weight and the final vowel is long (kasárō, qacámō, arátō, badárō); antepenult when the final vowel is short (wáqwaqe vs waqwáqō) or when the final is long but the penult is lighter than the antepenult (engángilō, ómborō, bárbarō, úšite, órobō, gúmitō). Final accent only in the negative imperative (hamáj/hamáy), the positive imperative of triradical verbs (saqár), the genitive ending -í (explained as an enclitic that keeps its own accent), and the loan name Amán.
2388.srule: Not mentioned in Reinisch 1888, Lautlehre section 31 'Der Accent' (separatum pp. 37-39, read in full): every example carries a single accent mark and no secondary or rhythmic accent is described.

2388.tone: Reinisch (1888) uses 'Accent', 'Ton' and 'Betonung' interchangeably and calls the rule a 'Tongesetz'; he does not distinguish stress from tone. Modern primary work analyses Kafa as a two-tone (H/L) language with the vowel mora as tone-bearing unit: Theil 2023 'Kafa' (Oxford Handbook of Ethiopian Languages), publisher abstract read via Crossref: 'The segmental phonology of Kafa is referenced on Theil (2007), while the tonology is based on Taddese (2001)... tones and gemination are not marked... major morphophonological processes range between gemination, tonal bridge effect, and absorption'; Taddese Habte Addo 1999/2001 and Azeb Amha 2017 (source list excerpt only) likewise treat Kafa as two-tone, and the Taddese excerpt says the earlier authors (Reinisch, Cerulli, Fleming) described 'stress' without being aware of tone. Conversely Cohen 1988 (open scan, p. 290, based on Cerulli 1951) states: 'Les documents publiés sur la variété de kafa considérée ici ne soulignent pas la présence de tons' and restates the accent rule moraically: 'Celui-ci porterait essentiellement sur la syllabe contenant la troisième more à partir de la fin du mot, toute syllabe en CV étant comptée pour une more et toute syllabe en CV: ou CVC pour deux mores. Des exceptions sont constituées par quelques suffixes, les uns portant toujours et les autres ne portant jamais l'accent.' No modern full text was reachable, so whether Kafa has word stress beside tone, or whether Reinisch's accent marks are H tones…

tn.quote: 2.4. Tons el accent. Les documents publiés sur la variété de kafa considérée ici ne soulignent pas la présence de tons. Cependant en motcha, parler appartenant au méme groupe, on a mis en relief l'existence d'un systéme de trois tonémes: un ton haut, un ton descendant et un ton bas, celui-ci ne pouvant porter que sur des voyelles longues (Leslau, 1959, voir ci-dessus $ 2.3.4.). Il n'est pas exclu qu'une enquéte particuliére sur ce point ne modifie les données utilisables aujourd'hui pour le kafa proprement dit.
tn.translation: 2.4. Tones and accent. The published documents on the variety of Kafa considered here do not point out the presence of tones. However, in Mocha, a lect belonging to the same group, the existence of a system of three tonemes has been brought out: a high tone, a falling tone and a low tone, the last able to fall only on long vowels (Leslau 1959, see above 2.3.4). It cannot be ruled out that a dedicated inquiry on this point would change the data usable today for Kafa proper.

2390.prule: No word-stress rule. Kagoro (Sébékoro) is a two-tone Manding language with two lexical tonal classes, A (rising lexical tone) and H (high), whose domain is the word, not the syllable. Vydrine's instrumental study of citation forms finds an incipient accent-like prominence whose locus is set by the tonal class, not by a word edge or by syllable weight: in class-H disyllables the first syllable predominates (pitch + intensity), in class-A disyllables the second syllable predominates (pitch + duration). The author states it is 'too early' to classify Kagoro as an accent language, though it is evolving in that direction (the mirror image of Mandinka, where class-H words carry the accent on the 2nd syllable).

2391.tone: Last 1886 says nothing about tone. Petzell 2015: 50 (open text in the copy consulted): 'There is a major difference between Kagulu and the majority of Bantu languages, and that is the lack of tones. In Kagulu, tones are not distinctive in meaning (neither lexical nor grammatical).' Kraska-Szlenk 2008: 96 (in the copy consulted) reports Petzell 2008: 41 second-hand: 'there is probably phrasal tone and not lexical tone', plus 'not very convincing claims about stress (the examples of rather unusual "pre-antepenult" stress on p. 41 could be perhaps cases of the initial stress)'.
